newsitem.title: UK: UK Labour's Blair slams Major for weak leadership.
newsitem.headline: UK Labour's Blair slams Major for weak leadership.

text.p: British opposition Labour leader Tony Blair said on Monday Prime Minister John Major had shown such pitiful leadership that Britain's influence in Europe and the wider world was at an all-time low.
Just 10 days before a general election on May 1, Blair used his only set-piece foreign policy speech of the campaign to argue that Labour alone could stand up for Britain's interests overseas.
"To negotiate well you have to have respect from those with whom you are negotiating. If you don't, you fail.

"And if you have neither the respect of those with whom you negotiate nor those on whose behalf you are negotiating, you fail abjectly. That is Mr Major's position," Blair said in his speech in the northern city of Manchester.

Major, 16 points behind in the latest opinion poll, hit back, accusing Blair of surrendering his negotiating position in advance of the June European Summit in Amsterdam and of stifling dissent in his own party with "stalinist" tactics.

Sticking to his message that only he was experienced enough to negotiate for Britain, Major said "(Europe) is becoming more centralist and all Conservatives oppose that centralised Europe and support our membership of a Europe of nation states."
He also shrugged off the polls, telling a London news conference: "This election is there to be won, of that I have not a shadow of doubt, and I believe we are going to win it."
Monday's Gallup poll in the Daily Telegraph newspaper showed the scale of the mountain Major has to climb to pull back Labour's lead and prevent an end to 18 years of Conservative rule.
Labour's advantage fell three points from Friday to 16, but they still hold 48 percent of the intended vote to 32 percent for the Conservatives.
After a weekend that saw leading members of Major's party at each other's throats over Britain's place in Europe, Blair could not resist a stream of withering personal invective.

He called Major's negotiating of the crisis over mad cow disease "a textbook of incompetence" and said it was an "undignified spectacle" for a prime minister to have to try to stop his party falling apart in the middle of an election.

Blair promised a fresh start in Europe and said the policy of perpetual isolation followed by the Conservatives since 1979 was misguided. He said he would stand up firmly for Britain's interests and was prepared to stand alone if necessary.

On the vexed question of Europe's planned single currency, due to be launched in January 1999, Blair repeated that he saw formidable obstacles to first wave entry and was sceptical about the chances of doing so any time in the next five years.
